analysis.one_liner: Closes offshore tax loopholes, taxes foreign corporations managed from the US, and requires country-by-country corporate tax disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two committees on the day it was introduced, received no hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets corporate offshore tax avoidance and financial secrecy. It would treat foreign corporations managed and controlled from the United States as domestic companies for tax purposes, tighten rules on corporate inversions, limit interest deductions by large multinational groups, tax swap payments sent offshore, and repeal accounting rules that let multinationals shift profits abroad. It would also require public companies to disclose profits and taxes paid country by country, give the Treasury power to penalize jurisdictions and banks that impede U.S. tax enforcement, and subject investment advisers and company-formation agents to anti-money-laundering rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who effectively make up tax revenue that large corporations and wealthy individuals shift offshore, and the IRS, which would get stronger tools to detect hidden offshore accounts.

how_it_helps.text: Treats foreign corporations whose management and control occur primarily in the United States as domestic for tax purposes, closing the loophole that lets companies be American in practice and foreign on paper.

Requires large public companies to disclose pre-tax profit and federal, state, and foreign taxes paid, on a country-by-country basis, in searchable public SEC filings — letting shareholders, journalists, and the public see who pays little tax and where.

Modifies inversion rules so that corporations that reincorporate abroad after acquiring a U.S. company are taxed as domestic if former U.S. owners hold more than 50 percent of the stock or management stays in the U.S.
Limits interest deductions for domestic members of large international reporting groups, curbing a common profit-shifting device in which debt is loaded onto U.S. entities.

Authorizes Treasury to restrict foreign jurisdictions and institutions that significantly impede U.S. tax enforcement, and creates rebuttable presumptions that assets and income moved through non-compliant offshore institutions belong to the U.S. person behind them.
Applies anti-money-laundering requirements to investment advisers and to businesses that form shell corporations, blocking common channels for hiding money offshore.

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational corporations using offshore structures, tax-haven banks and secrecy jurisdictions, investment advisers, shell-company formation agents, and wealthy individuals with hidden offshore accounts.

drawbacks.text: The rebuttable presumptions would treat money flowing through non-FATCA institutions as taxable income of the U.S. person behind it, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence — a heavy burden that could sweep in some taxpayers with legitimate foreign arrangements and impose costly compliance on financial firms.

The interest-deduction limit applies to any international group with over $100 million in gross receipts and could raise financing costs for large U.S.-based multinational operations, some of which might be passed to consumers or reflected in reduced investment.
Country-by-country disclosure imposes new detailed reporting on every public company filing annual and quarterly reports, with compliance costs concentrated on large multinationals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is aimed squarely at tax avoidance by large corporations and hidden offshore wealth, with the revenue and fairness gains falling to ordinary taxpayers. The main costs are compliance burdens on large financial firms and the risk that broad presumptions penalize some legitimate foreign activity; those costs are real but modest compared with the scale of offshore avoidance the bill targets. The design is aggressive but not careless — it includes exclusions, regulatory discretion, and court oversight for expanded summons projects.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services Committees the day it was introduced and never received any further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on March 13, 2019, with 46 Democratic cosponsors joining at introduction.
The Speaker referred it to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, the House Financial Services Committee for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion action in the Senate before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations using offshore tax structures, tax-haven banks and secrecy jurisdictions, and wealthy individuals with hidden offshore accounts kept the status quo — no new reporting, no new presumption rules, no anti-money-laundering obligations for investment advisers and shell-company formation agents.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act on March 13, 2019.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the entire two-year Congress, leaving it without action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were Democrats — none of the 197 House Republicans signed on — and the bill never advanced past committee referral in the Democratic-majority House.

industries.note: The bill would treat U.S.-managed foreign corporations as domestic for tax, curb inversions, limit interest-shifting deductions, and tax swap payments sent offshore — directly reducing tools used to move profits out of the U.S. tax base. Its defeat preserves those structures at ordinary taxpayers' expense.

industries.industry: Tax-haven banks and offshore financial centers
industries.note: Treasury could impose restrictions on jurisdictions and institutions that impede U.S. tax enforcement, and assets held through non-compliant institutions would be presumed controlled by and taxable to the U.S. person behind them.

industries.industry: Company formation agents and investment advisers
industries.note: Both would face anti-money-laundering program, reporting, and customer-identification duties for the first time, closing channels used to set up anonymous shell entities and manage offshore money.

Investment companies with $50 million or more in assets under management that are managed primarily from the U.S. would be taxed as domestic corporations even if organized abroad, changing how funds and investment vehicles are structured.
Country-by-country disclosure of profits, employees, and taxes paid would raise compliance costs but also give investors and the public visibility into where profits sit and where taxes go.
